title: The Opera Game
black: Duke Karl of Brunswick and Count Isouard
summary: The Opera Game, played by Paul Morphy in Paris in 1858, is remembered for its brilliant attack: White sacrifices material to open the d-file and the Black king never escapes the centre. Watch how Black's natural-looking moves, especially 9...b5 and 10...cxb5, hand White the open lines, and how the finish of 16.Qb8+ and 17.Rd8# ends the game on the back rank.

moves.comment: 1.e4 claims the centre and opens lines for the queen and the bishop on f1.
1...e5 mirrors White, contesting the centre and opening the diagonal for Black's dark-squared bishop.
2.Nf3 develops and attacks the e5 pawn, a simple way to put pressure on Black's centre.
2...d6 defends e5 solidly, graded good, though the engine preferred 2...Nc6, which develops with more purpose.
3.d4 builds a broad pawn centre and strikes again at the e5 pawn.
3...Bg4 pressures the knight on f3, graded good; the engine preferred 3...Nd7 as the calmer development.
4.dxe5 takes the pawn and opens the d-file, graded good; the engine preferred 4.Nc3 to keep more control.
4...Bxf3 trades off Black's bishop for the knight, graded an inaccuracy, because it lets White's queen recapture on f3 with a fine centre.
5.Qxf3 recaptures, centralising the queen and eyeing the f7 pawn along the diagonal.
5...dxe5 recaptures the pawn, leaving the d-file fully open for both sides.
6.Bc4 points the bishop at f7 and the cramped Black king; graded good, though 6.Qb3 was preferred.
6...Nf6 develops, but is graded a mistake; the engine preferred 6...Qf6, and the evaluation jumps by nearly two pawns.

moment.title: Development that loosened the grip
moment.text: Black's 6...Nf6 is graded a mistake and the evaluation jumps from +1.6 to +3.4. The engine preferred 6...Qf6, which keeps the queen guarding the kingside and avoids the pin that follows. Notice how a natural developing move can still hand the opponent a strong initiative.

moves.comment: 7.Qb3 brings the queen to a strong square, hitting b7 and lining up against f7.
7...Qe7 defends f7 and keeps the position together, graded best.
8.Nc3 develops the last minor piece, graded good; the engine preferred the greedy 8.Qxb7.
8...c6 is solid and prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop on c4.
9.Bg5 pins the knight on f6 against the queen on e7, adding pressure on the centre and the king.
9...b5 chases the bishop but weakens Black's king, graded a mistake; the engine preferred 9...Kd8.

moment.title: The pawn push that weakened the king
moment.text: 9...b5 is graded a mistake, and the evaluation moves from +2.8 to +5.2. It chases the bishop, but it also opens the Black king's queenside cover. The engine preferred 9...Kd8, showing that the king itself could have been moved to safety first.

moves.comment: 10.Nxb5 sacrifices a knight to open lines against the black king, graded best.
10...cxb5 accepts the offer, graded an inaccuracy; the engine preferred 10...Qb4+ to counter-attack.

moment.title: Accepting the sacrifice
moment.text: 10...cxb5 is graded an inaccuracy as the evaluation rises to +7.4. Black accepts the knight but leaves the king on the open file with White's bishop to follow with check. The engine's preferred 10...Qb4+ was a counter-check, which is a useful reminder to look for checks first when under attack.

moves.comment: 11.Bxb5+ checks the king with the bishop, keeping the attack going along the open lines.
11...Nbd7 blocks the check with a knight, graded good; the engine preferred 11...Kd8.
12.O-O-O castles queenside, bringing the rook towards the open d-file, graded best.
12...Rd8 contests the d-file, graded good; the engine preferred 12...Rb8 for the rook on b8.
13.Rxd7 exchanges a rook for the knight, opening the d-file further, graded best.
13...Rxd7 recaptures, graded good; the engine preferred 13...Nxd7 to keep the rook back.

moment.title: Trading into the open file
moment.text: The exchange of rooks on d7 and the d-file trade open the position completely. White keeps the file, and Black's remaining defenders become overloaded. Look for how each recapture changes which pieces are guarding the king.

moves.comment: 14.Rd1 doubles rooks on the d-file, piling pressure on the pinned knight on d7, graded best.
14...Qe6 is graded good, though the engine preferred 14...Qb4 to challenge the attack.
15.Bxd7+ takes the knight with check, removing a key defender of the king.
15...Nxd7 recaptures, graded good, but the engine shows that 15...Qxd7 was better and that this allows mate in two.

moment.title: The recapture that allowed mate
moment.text: 15...Nxd7 is graded good, but the evaluation moves from +10.1 to mate in two. The engine's line with 15...Qxd7 keeps the queen on the defence and avoids the back-rank trap. A recapture that ignores the back rank can be decisive.

moves.comment: 16.Qb8+ gives check with the queen, forcing the knight to capture and clearing the back rank.
16...Nxb8 is forced, since the knight on d7 must take the queen on b8.
17.Rd8# delivers mate on the back rank, with the king boxed in by its own pieces.

moment.title: Back-rank mate ends the game
moment.text: 17.Rd8# is the final blow, delivered along the open d-file. Black's own pieces on the back rank, the queen gone and the knight pinned to the defence, leave the king with no escape. It is a classic pattern worth memorising.

lessons: When your opponent gives up material to open lines, check every forcing move for both sides before you develop quietly.
Keep an eye on your back rank and your king's escape squares, especially after pieces are traded or pinned.
Recapture with the piece that keeps your king safest, since the wrong recapture can turn a holdable position into mate.
